chunks: Al-Hasan ibn al-Abbas al-Ma'rufi wrote to al-Ridha (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom! Inform me: what is the difference between the Messenger, the Prophet, and the Imam?'

He said — so he wrote, or said: 'The difference between the Messenger, the Prophet, and the Imam is that the Messenger is one unto whom Jibrail descends; he sees him and hears his speech, and the Revelation is sent down to him, and sometimes he sees in his dream something like the dream of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). The Prophet sometimes hears the speech and sometimes sees the figure but does not hear. And the Imam is one who hears the speech but does not see the figure.'

key_terms.الرَّسُولُ: Messenger — one who receives a new divine law and is commissioned to deliver it; has full two-way sensory contact with Jibrail
key_terms.النَّبِيُّ: Prophet — receives divine guidance but either hears without seeing Jibrail or sees without hearing
key_terms.الْإِمَامُ: Imam — the divinely guided leader after the Prophet, hears divine speech without seeing the angelic figure
key_terms.الْوَحْيُ: Wahy — divine Revelation, the formal descent of sacred knowledge from God
key_terms.جَبْرَئِيلُ: Jibrail — the Angel of Revelation, intermediary between God and His messengers
key_terms.رُؤْيَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ: The dream-vision of Ibrahim — a reference to the dream in which Ibrahim (AS) was shown the command to sacrifice his son

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a Rasool, a Nabi, and an Imam according to Imam al-Ridha in Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a formal doctrinal distinction between three ranks of divine communication: the Rasool (Messenger), the Nabi (Prophet), and the Imam. Imam al-Ridha (AS) explains that these three offices differ in their mode of receiving divine guidance — the Messenger receives full sensory contact with Jibrail including vision and audition; the Prophet receives either one but not both; while the Imam receives only the auditory channel without visual perception. This question was posed by al-Hasan ibn al-Abbas al-Ma'rufi in written correspondence, reflecting the theological curiosity of the early Shia scholarly circles in clarifying the nature of divine communication to uphold the Imam's unique spiritual authority without equating it to prophethood.
